items.title: PINE: Point, Instance and Normal Estimation in One-Step Diffusion Model
items.summary: Understanding a scene requires both geometry and semantics: geometry recovers its spatial structure, and semantics separates it into objects. Current models obtain the two from…
items.abstract: Understanding a scene requires both geometry and semantics: geometry recovers its spatial structure, and semantics separates it into objects. Current models obtain the two from separate networks or separate passes. We present PINE, a one-step Omni Diffusion Transformer that predicts the point map, the surface normals, and the instance map of an image in one forward pass. PINE treats each map as a token stream, and a stream mask decides which streams interact. A camera-aware ray encoding positions every token by its camera ray rather than its pixel. Grounding attention adds the affinity of pretrained DINOv3 features to the attention logits. Trained on only 139K synthetic images for geometry, PINE achieves state-of-the-art point maps whether or not intrinsics are given and the best average rank on surface normals. It also exceeds SAM on large objects with less than 1 percent of its training images, and it predicts all three maps 5.7x faster than MoGe-3 with SAM.

items.title: Align the Pair, Not the Sample: Representation Alignment for Faster and Better One-Step Generato
items.summary: Representation alignment markedly accelerates diffusion training, but one-step generators raise a question that diffusion does not: which training path should receive the loss? A one-step…
items.aiSummary: In one-step generator training, aligning the paired reconstruction path rather than the generative path improves recall and sample quality while accelerating both training stages and lowering FID.
items.abstract: Representation alignment markedly accelerates diffusion training, but one-step generators raise a question that diffusion does not: which training path should receive the loss? A one-step generator sees two kinds of inputs. Corrupted real images come with their clean counterpart, which provides an instance-paired target. Samples generated from pure noise have no corresponding real image, yet this is where the final model operates. We study this question on Priming, which trains one-step generators from scratch by reconstructing corrupted images and then matching feature distributions with optimal transport. Aligning the generative path, the natural choice, collapses recall (0.45!to!0.15--0.25) in all 17 configurations we test, including five target constructions and loss weights down to 0.05. Aligning the paired reconstruction path with a frozen DINOv2 encoder instead helps in every setting we test. A short analysis explains this asymmetry: when the target carries no instance information about the input, the optimal aligned feature is constant within each class, so the loss pulls samples toward class prototypes. A control confirms this: aligning the paired path to a random same-class image instead of the input's own image removes most of the gain. Inside the generator, paired-path alignment creates an interface block through which post-training routes noise, and the image semantics carried through it predict sample quality across 16 models. The resulting recipe, \method, accelerates both training stages on ImageNet 256!times!256: it matches the 160-epoch baseline with 2times fewer priming epochs, surpasses its final quality with 4times fewer post-training updates, and lowers FID to 1.30 (B) and 1.155 (L) at the standard budget. A joint single-stage variant trains native one-step generators and reaches FID 1.22 with 115M parameters.

items.title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images
items.summary: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location,…
items.abstract: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.

items.title: PhyCoVE: Benchmarking Physical Counterfactual Video Editing across Diverse Material Dynamics
items.summary: Physical counterfactual video editing turns a source video and a language-specified physical edit at a given execution frame into a counterfactual video that shows how…
items.aiSummary: PhyCoVE, a 533-case benchmark, and counterfactual fidelity evaluate video editing models on physical counterfactual edits involving rigid, elastic, and fluid dynamics, showing that even the best model reproduces only about one seventh of the physical change.
items.abstract: Physical counterfactual video editing turns a source video and a language-specified physical edit at a given execution frame into a counterfactual video that shows how the scene would evolve after the edit. Existing evaluations with counterfactual target videos mainly cover object removal or specific rigid-body motions, although real scenes also involve elastic deformation, fluid flow, and interactions among rigid bodies, elastic solids, and fluids. We introduce PhyCoVE, a benchmark of 533 cases on 110 source videos that covers rigid, elastic, and fluid dynamics in five interaction patterns, with edits that remove an object, change a physical quantity, or insert a new object. For the simulated cases, a language model proposes scene designs, coding agents build them with solvers suited to each material and physically based rendering and then simulate each edit from the source scene state, and humans check every stage. For the real cases, we record continuously from one camera position before and after each edit. We also propose counterfactual fidelity, a metric that applies across materials and their interactions and measures how much of the physical change from the source video to the target video a generated video reproduces. We evaluate seven open-source and commercial video editing models and find that counterfactual fidelity ranks them nearly as human preference does, but even the best model reproduces only about one seventh of the physical change. The models change how a scene looks but rarely how it evolves, whereas a physical edit requires understanding the dynamics that it changes. Physical counterfactual video editing thus remains far from solved, and PhyCoVE provides a foundation for developing and evaluating methods for it.

items.title: KernelShift: Benchmarking Kernel Optimization Across Evolving Hardware
items.summary: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor…
items.aiSummary: A benchmarking pipeline evaluates coding agents on optimizing CPU kernels across evolving Arm architectural extensions, showing strong gains on established SIMD extensions but unreliable adaptation to newer matrix-tile programming models.
items.abstract: Efficient AI computation depends on hardware that evolves over time, shifting the strategies needed to implement performant code. For CPU kernels, a key evolving factor is the set of available architectural extensions, which expose specialized hardware instructions that change the techniques used to optimize kernels. We study how effectively coding agents use these new, potentially unfamiliar extensions to write fast code. We introduce KernelShift, a benchmarking pipeline and a set of environments for evaluating coding agents in kernel optimization across evolving CPU architectures. Its agent-assisted, human-verified pipeline turns code repositories into benchmark instances, and its environments let agents optimize code with feedback from the target hardware. Using this pipeline, we construct 99 kernels from real-world, actively developed repositories (ncnn, llama.cpp, Arm SIMD Loops, and KleidiAI), including inference workloads derived from real model executions. KernelShift supports incorporating new kernels and hardware configurations as libraries and processors evolve. We evaluate agents with proprietary and open-weight models across progressively newer architectural extensions (Arm Neon, SVE, SVE2, and SME2), examining how performance changes as hardware evolves. On established extensions, agents beat the auto-vectorized compiler everywhere (2.4-19.8x) and exceed general-purpose libraries such as ncnn (getting up to 2.74x over its Neon kernels), but fall behind Arm's hand-tuned KleidiAI kernels (0.70x). In end-to-end inference of two LLMs, agent-written kernels achieve a 1.3-1.6x prefill speedup over llama.cpp's fast path. However, current agents do not yet reliably adapt to new extensions that require unfamiliar programming models, such as SME2's matrix tiles.

items.title: transformers · Release v5.24.0
items.summary: # Release v5.24.0 ## New Model additions ### Inkling 2 Mini Inkling 2 Mini is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text…
items.releaseNotes: # Release v5.24.0 ## New Model additions ### Inkling 2 Mini Inkling 2 Mini is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs. It is a smaller sibling of Inkling 2 Small, added in v5.23.0. It has 24 decoder layers instead of 48, and compensates with a looping mechanism in which layers 6 to 17 run three times. A learned message-passing mechanism mixes the residuals of the previous pass into the attention and mixture-of-experts inputs of each loop layer. The decoder has a hidden size of 2304 and routes each token to 8 of 128 experts. The image encoder, tokenizer and processor are the same as Inkling 2 Small's. A research checkpoint ([TML-d24-varloop-research](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/TML-d24-varloop-research)) has the same architecture but supports a variable number of loop passes. Fewer passes are faster, and more passes improve quality. Both checkpoints contain NVFP4 and MXFP8 quantized layers, which are dequantized at load time. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/inkling2_loop) | [Blog Post](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/) | [HF Blog Post](https://huggingface.co/blog/inkling2mini) * Add Inkling2 Mini (#51050) by @guarin ### Apertus 1.5 Apertus 1.5 is a multimodal model from the Swiss AI Initiative that accepts text, images and audio and generates text. It extends the Apertus language model with the EMU3.5 vision tokenizer for images and WavTokenizer for audio. The EMU3.5 tokenizer is an image-only VQGAN with the same encoder as Chameleon's, and it assigns codes by the largest inner product with the codebook. The media tokenizers turn images and audio into discrete tokens, which the language backbone processes alongside text in a shared input vocabulary. The output vocabulary contains only text tokens, so image and audio generation are not supported. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/apertus1p5) * Apertus 1.5: add model (#47662) by @RaphaelKreft ### WavTokenizer WavTokenizer encodes 24 kHz mono audio into discrete tokens using a single codebook, at 40 or 75 tokens per second depending on the checkpoint, and reconstructs audio from those tokens. `WavTokenizerModel` encodes and decodes, and `WavTokenizerEncoderModel` only encodes. Speech, music/audio and unified checkpoints are available. The 40-token-per-second variant is the audio tokenizer of Apertus 1.5. Training the codec is not supported. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/wavtokenizer) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2408.16532) * Apertus 1.5: add model (#47662) by @RaphaelKreft ### Dory Dory is a looped (latent-recurrent) language model from NVIDIA. It uses a normalized-GPT architecture with interleaved sliding-window and full attention layers. A shared block of layers is applied repeatedly, so Dory can spend more compute per token. The loop count can be changed at inference time on the same checkpoint to trade speed against quality. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/dory) | [Paper (nGPT)](https://huggingface.co/papers/2410.01131) * Add Dory model support (#50099) by @shan18 ### HY4-VL HY4-VL (Hunyuan V4 Vision-Language) combines the HYV4 mixture-of-experts text backbone with a vision encoder for image-text and video-text generation. It supports dynamic-resolution visual inputs and uses multimodal rotary position embeddings (mRoPE) to represent temporal and spatial positions. It builds on the Qwen2-VL design and shares its vision patch merger with HunYuan-VL. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/hy_v4_vl) * Add HY4-VL (#50877) by @vasqu ### Omnilingual ASR Omnilingual ASR is a suite of multilingual speech-recognition models from Meta FAIR that covers more than 1,600 languages. Each model pairs a Wav2Vec2-style audio encoder with one of two heads: * **CTC** (`OmniASRForCTC`): a linear projection to the vocabulary, decoded non-autoregressively with greedy CTC. * **Audio language model** (`OmniASRForConditionalGeneration`): audio embeddings are projected into a Llama decoder that generates the transcription. It optionally takes a language code (e.g. `"eng_Latn"`), which generally improves transcription quality. Both variants come in 300M, 1B, 3B and 7B sizes. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/omniasr) | [CTC Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/omniasr_ctc) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2511.09690) * Adding Omnilingual ASR models (#43265) by @ebezzam ### Lara Mini Lara Mini is a multilingual base language model from Translated with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters per token. It is a hybrid of linear-time recurrent layers, sliding-window attention and a few global attention layers, each followed by a fine-grained mixture of experts. The weights are released under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license (non-commercial use) in a gated repository. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/lara_mini) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2611.16956) * Add Lara Mini (#50819) by @ValeGian ### SarvamMLA SarvamMLA is the architecture of Sarvam-105B, a 105B-parameter mixture-of-experts language model from Sarvam AI. It combines Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with sparse MoE routing: 128 routed experts with 8 active per token, plus 1 shared expert. It uses sigmoid routing with group-based top-k selection and YaRN rotary embeddings for contexts up to 131K tokens. The architecture is the same as DeepSeek-V3, with a custom configuration. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/sarvam_mla) * Add SarvamMLA model (sarvamai/sarvam-105b) (#44569) by @aashay-sarvam ### SarvamMoE SarvamMoE is the architecture of Sarvam-30B, Sarvam AI's 30B-parameter mixture-of-experts model. It uses grouped-query attention with QK normalization, and 128 routed experts with 6 active per token, plus 1 shared expert. The architecture is the same as GLM-4-MoE, so the auto classes load it with the GLM-4-MoE implementation and only `SarvamMoEConfig` is specific to SarvamMoE. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/sarvam_moe) * Add SarvamMoE (sarvamai/sarvam-30b) (#51023) by @hmellor ### EXAONE EXAONE covers the EXAONE 3.0, EXAONE 3.5 and EXAONE Deep language models from LG AI Research. Their architecture is the same as Llama, so the auto classes load them with `LlamaModel` and `LlamaForCausalLM`, and only `ExaoneConfig` is specific to EXAONE. The released checkpoints are renamed to the Llama names when loading and back when saving, so they no longer need `trust_remote_code=True`. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/exaone) * Add EXAONE (#50966) by @hmellor ### Model updates * **Ling 3.1 Flash** now loads natively through `BailingHybrid`, like Ling 3.0 in v5.20.0 (#49737) by @icavan * **Beam** gains a `BeamForTokenClassification` head (#50634) by @AymenKallala ## Breaking changes ### Cache renaming: `past_key_values` / `cache_params` → `cache` (#50585, #50730) `past_key_values` and `cache_params` are renamed to `cache` across the library. The old names still work with a deprecation warning; see the dedicated section below. * 🚨🚨 Rename `past_key_values`/`cache_params` to `cache` (#50585) by @Cyrilvallez * Bump minimal peft version for cache name compatibility (#50730) by @Cyrilvallez Attention models used to call their cache `past_key_values`, while Mamba-style and linear-attention models called it `cache_params`. Hybrid models therefore had to juggle two names for the same object. There is now a single name, `cache`, everywhere: model `forward` signatures, `generate`, `prepare_inputs_for_generation`, the masking utilities, and every `ModelOutput`. ```python # Before outputs = model(input_ids, past_key_values=past_key_values, use_cache=True) next_cache = outputs.past_key_values # Now outputs = model(input_ids, cache=cache, use_cache=True) next_cache = outputs.cache ``` * **Fully backward compatible for now**: `past_key_values=` / `cache_params=` are renamed to `cache` automatically, with a one-time deprecation warning. Model `forward` and `prepare_inputs_for_generation` accept the old names until **v5.40.0**, and `generate` accepts them until **v6.0.0**. Passing both an old name and `cache` raises a `ValueError`. * **Outputs too**: `outputs.past_key_values`, `outputs.cache_params` and `outputs["past_key_values"]` still return the cache. Output classes can also still be built with the old field names (e.g. `CausalLMOutputWithPast(past_key_values=...)`), so most remote-code models keep working unchanged. * **Custom code**: models defined outside the library should rename their arguments to `cache`. Layers now call `cache.update(key_states, value_states, layer_idx, kwargs=kwargs)`, so custom `Cache` subclasses that override `update` should accept the extra `kwargs` argument. 🚨 `peft>=0.22.0` is now required. 📚 Docs: ### Multimodal Outputs Generative multimodal models now return shared output classes (`MultimodalBaseModelOutputWithPast`, `MultimodalCausalLMOutputWithPast`, and their MoE variants) instead of one output class per model. Code that checks for a model-specific output class should switch to these. * 🚨 Multimodal Model Output for generative LMs (#50379) by @zucchini-nlp `modeling_attn_mask_utils.py` has been removed. Every function in it had been deprecated in favor of `transformers.masking_utils`. Remote-code models that still import `_prepare_4d_causal_attention_mask` or `AttentionMaskConverter` from it must move to `transformers.masking_utils`. ### Other things * Remove deprecated and unused older mask API file (#50728) by @Cyrilvallez LayoutLMv3 (and the PP-DocLayoutV2 reading-order model that shares its code) now go through the attention interface, so SDPA and flex attention are supported. The relative position bias is built once per forward pass and passed to attention as `position_bias`. * 🚨 LayoutLMv3: support SDPA through the attention interface, build the relative position bias once (#50688) by @14H034160212 ## Cache Beyond the rename, this release adds static-cache support to assisted decoding and fixes `generate` with flex attention and a static cache. `StaticCache` now allocates values with the value states' dtype, and the cache is kept under activation checkpointing when gradients are off. The `is_linear` / `is_croppable` properties are fixed for hybrid linear/full-attention models, BigBird block-sparse decoding works with a KV cache, and KV sharing is restored for the Gemma 4 assistants. * Support static cache in assisted decoding (#49415) by @jiqing-feng * Simplify cache handling in generate (#50910) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix generate with flex attention and a static cache (#50864) by @tarekziade * Allocate the StaticCache values with the value states' dtype (#49554) by @qgallouedec * Keep the cache under activation checkpointing when gradients are off (#50890) by @qgallouedec * [cache] Fix is_linear property to correctly remove hybrid layers (#51030) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix is_croppable property for mixed linear-full attention classes (#51028) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix BigBird block-sparse decoding with a KV cache (#49984) by @jiqing-feng * fix(gemma4): Restore KV sharing for the Gemma 4 assistants and their targets (#50531) by @harshaljanjani * Fix Dory vocabulary resizing, loop validation, and last-loop static caching (#50982) by @shan18 * Fix device placement in `test_bc_cache_name_{forward,generate}` (#50757) by @ydshieh * Update test_dynamic_cache_hard expected values for A10G (#50822) by @ydshieh ## Generation Generation fixes cover sampled beam search (candidates are sorted again before finalization), constrained sampling (batch IDs are preserved), `generate` on MPS with encoder-decoder models, and `TextStreamer`, which no longer drops spaces or lags on text without spaces such as Chinese, Japanese and Korean. `StopStringCriteria` initializes faster, and its cache now actually hits. * Restore sorting of sampled beam candidates before finalization (#50754) by @BlazeSR10hawk * fix(generate): preserve batch IDs in constrained sampling (#50883) by @BlazeSR10hawk * Fix generate for mps and encoder-decoder models (#51032) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix TextStreamer dropping spaces sometimes (#51036) by @Cyrilvallez * Fix long lagging when streaming text without spaces and NJK chars (#36708) by @CNSeniorious000 * Speed up StopStringCriteria init and fix its cache never hitting (#50780) by @TheNetherWatcher ## Continuous batching Continuous batching now works under `torch.inference_mode()` and finds sharded key/value projections under any decoder path. The per-token memory estimate scales with the TP size, warmup handles async and static inputs correctly, and an out-of-bounds error in the top-k processor is fixed. * [CB] Scale the per-token memory estimate by the TP size (#48566) by @qgallouedec * Continuous batching: find the sharded key/value projections under any decoder path (#50366) by @qgallouedec * Fix continuous batching under torch.inference_mode() (#50863) by @tarekziade * [CB] Re-order the warmup block so async warms both sets of inputs (#50868) by @remi-or * Wait for each warmup forward before the next one rewrites the static inputs (#50353) by @qgallouedec * Fix out-of-bounds error in continuous batching top-k processor (#50282) by @khush-patel-09 * [CB] Replace test prompts with less ambiguous ones (#50876) by @remi-or ## Chat templates, parsing and serving Chat parsing gets a new `python-call-list` content parser, better handling of bare keys and duplicate XML arguments, and three further parser fixes. `apply_chat_template` accepts message objects, and assistant masks are correct with left truncation. `transformers serve` handles a missing Hub cache, lists loaded models in `/v1/models`, keeps local paths containing `@`, and keeps assistant content when `tool_calls` is empty. * [Chat Parsing] Add `python-call-list` content parser (#50619) by @nico-martin * [Chat Parsing] Quote bare keys that have whitespace around them with `unquoted_keys` (#50917) by @gagan-baghel * [Chat Parsing] Preserve array values when merging duplicate XML arguments (#50760) by @crunz-ailab * Fix three chat parsing bugs (#50655) by @Rocketknight1 * Fix apply_chat_template with message objects (#50818) by @Rocketknight1 * Fix assistant tokens mask with left truncation (#50758) by @yibol9768-alt * fix(chat templating): isolate concurrent assistant tracking (#50673) by @BlazeSR10hawk * Just a small improvement in jinja (#50635) by @zucchini-nlp * Accept argument types in parentheses in get_json_schema docstrings (#50745) by @miinimal * [serve] Handle missing Hub cache and include loaded models in /v1/models (#50663) by @RyanMullins * [serve] Preserve local model paths containing '@' in ModelManager (#50662) by @RyanMullins * [serve] Keep assistant content when tool_calls is null or empty (#50707) by @AabhasK ## Pipelines Multimodal pipelines now accept media-only inputs and string assistant prefills, keep Mistral prefills in Voxtral, stop mutating generation kwargs, and return chat messages as `input_text` when returning tensors. `pipeline` also respects a `device_map` that targets a single device. * fix(pipelines)

items.title: KMed-31B Technical Report
items.summary: We present KMed-31B, a medical large language model post-trained from an open-weight model for on-premises deployment with limited hardware. Post-training a model for diverse medical…
items.abstract: We present KMed-31B, a medical large language model post-trained from an open-weight model for on-premises deployment with limited hardware. Post-training a model for diverse medical tasks remains difficult, because improving one kind of task can lower performance on another. We attribute this to differences between tasks in expected output and available feedback. Medical question answering and diagnosis prediction have reference answers, whereas clinical inquiry has no single correct response and is judged with rubrics. We therefore divide medical training tasks into four categories by these two properties, train one specialist per category with a reward that its feedback supports, and integrate the specialists into a single student with Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD^2). For clinical inquiry, we build Synthetic Health Dialogue, a simulated corpus of consultations with lay users and clinicians whose patient cases span common clinical presentations in primary care. Relative to its base model, KMed-31B raises HealthBench Hard from 22.95 to 41.87 and HealthBench Professional from 37.92 to 50.20 in non-thinking mode, and from 23.80 to 51.48 and from 41.97 to 59.18 in thinking mode, while its scores on four multiple-choice medical benchmarks are maintained or slightly improved. KMed-31B has the highest unadjusted HealthBench Hard score among the compared models, including proprietary ones, and scores higher on HealthBench Professional than every open-weight model we compare, including models with more than ten times as many total parameters. Applied to another base model, Qwen3.8-27B, the same training recipe also raises both HealthBench scores. We describe the training recipe, data construction, and settings in detail so that institutions requiring on-premises deployment can develop medical models from open-weight foundations.

items.title: Don't Sleep, Keep Watch: Proactive Perception for Computer-Use Agents
items.summary: Computer-use agents (CUAs) built on vision-language models are increasingly entrusted with long-horizon tasks in live desktop, web, and mobile environments, where the screen keeps changing…
items.aiSummary: NightWatch adds a lightweight streaming watcher to vision-language computer-use agents to keep perception synchronized with dynamic interfaces, reducing latency and wasted time while maintaining or improving task success.
items.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) built on vision-language models are increasingly entrusted with long-horizon tasks in live desktop, web, and mobile environments, where the screen keeps changing on its own. However, current CUAs lack real-time situational awareness: they perceive the environment through discrete snapshots, and the substantial inference latency of VLMs, compounded by highly dynamic interfaces, opens a perception-action gap in which the observed state frequently becomes stale before the corresponding action is executed. To bridge this gap, we present NightWatch, a plug-and-play framework that endows any CUA with continuous, temporally grounded perception without changing the agent's model, prompt, or action space. NightWatch couples the VLM agent with NightWatch-0.8B, a lightweight System-1 model that performs streaming monitoring of the interface state and keeps the agent synchronized with the evolving environment at low computational cost and latency, thereby grounding each decision in the current state rather than an outdated snapshot and reducing both stale actions and idle waiting while preserving task success. Experiments on desktop and dynamic web environments (OSWorld-Verified and DynaCU-Bench) show that NightWatch, driven by a watcher of only 0.8B parameters, reduces non-reasoning wall-clock time by 33% and wasted time by 53% on OSWorld while keeping task success on par, raises success on DynaCU-Bench from 39.5% to 44.2% with the large VLM agent, and is more efficient than passive-watching baselines such as AOI and PUSV under the same screenshot-only input, as well as a System-1 decision model more than 30times its size. Overall, NightWatch demonstrates that the timing of perception is as critical as its content, marking a step toward agents that maintain continuous awareness of their environment rather than perceiving it turn by turn.

items.title: S-Mind: Internalizing Multi-View Geometry for Spatial Intelligence
items.summary: Spatial intelligence, the ability to reason about 3D space from visual observations, becomes essential as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) move into the physical world.…
items.abstract: Spatial intelligence, the ability to reason about 3D space from visual observations, becomes essential as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) move into the physical world. Beyond perceiving each view, it rests on two cornerstones of human cognition: fusing multiple views into one coherent 3D scene and mentally transforming that scene to new viewpoints as reasoning unfolds. Yet our spatial probes reveal that MLLMs largely lack both capabilities, even after spatial fine-tuning. We therefore present S-Mind, which internalizes multi-view geometry within the MLLM through a compact set of spatial tokens. It supervises these tokens to hold the fused 3D scene and re-emits them to re-express this scene from every viewpoint the reasoning adopts. Across four spatial benchmarks, S-Mind improves its Qwen3.5 backbones by up to 22.26 points and surpasses frontier general models such as GPT-6-Astra (+0.45), Kimi-K3.1-Pro (+1.97), and GLM-5.3-Flash (+7.80) in average accuracy. Moreover, the same probes confirm that it acquires both capabilities, reaching fusion and transformation accuracies of 65.11% and 82.17%, against at most 16.02% and 37.28% for the baselines. At inference, S-Mind also runs about 100x faster than a tool-based agent on the same backbone. Instilled through these spatial tokens during training, spatial capability becomes intrinsic to the backbone and persists even when the tokens are withheld, offering a promising path toward spatial intelligence in MLLMs.

items.title: EvoViM: Recursively Self-Evolving Visual Agents for Exploration with Deferred Queries
items.summary: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring…
items.aiSummary: EvoViM lets frozen multimodal agents recursively evolve a pixel-level visual program from interaction experience, improving deferred-query visual reasoning and sequential decision-making over strong baselines.
items.abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.

VideoJSON: A Minimal Harness Beats Purpose-Built Memory for Ultra-Long Video Understanding
items.summary: Answering questions over days or weeks of video requires searching for scattered clues across long timelines. Existing video agents rely on complex memory graphs and…
items.abstract: Answering questions over days or weeks of video requires searching for scattered clues across long timelines. Existing video agents rely on complex memory graphs and fixed retrieval pipelines, which restrict how the agent can search. We propose VideoJSON, a minimal harness for ultra-long video understanding that keeps the memory simple and lets a coding agent write its own search programs. During indexing, a vision-language model turns each minute of video into a single JSON record containing a dense caption and structured fields such as events, entities, places, and speech transcripts. At query time, the agent writes Python or Bash programs in a sandboxed container to filter, link, and read these records over multiple steps, without task-specific training or raw video access. On four ultra-long video benchmarks, VideoJSON with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash outperforms MAGIC-Video by 7.0, 20.0, and 24.75 points on EgoLifeQA, Ego-R1-Bench, and MM-Lifelong Week, and beats the best prior EgoMemReason score by 12.6 points. Across four policy models of increasing capability, VideoJSON's average score rises by up to 11.58 points over the weakest model, compared with at most 5.50 points for MAGIC-Video. Ablations show that both agentic code search and the structured JSON records drive these gains, while adding hourly summaries, extra tools, or video access changes the average score by less than 1.5 points. In addition, fine-tuning Qwen-3.5-Flash on 64 VideoJSON trajectories from an unrelated 100-hour livestream improves its MM-Lifelong scores by up to 8.25 points. Code will be open-sourced after publication.

items.title: HEP-Ex-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Performance in High Energy Physics Experiment Data Analyses with Sealed Worlds
items.summary: Agentic systems are increasingly being explored for automating experimental high-energy physics measurements, but the correctness of their results can today be reliably evaluated only via…
items.abstract: Agentic systems are increasingly being explored for automating experimental high-energy physics measurements, but the correctness of their results can today be reliably evaluated only via extensive expert review. To address this, we propose a method to perform detailed quantitative evaluations of agent-driven analyses through the use of blind analysis and injection tests, which are critical in a typical expert review. Agents develop a data analysis pipeline on a public dataset, while the evaluation is performed on programmatically generated sealed private datasets where signals are injected and simulation settings varied within realistic detector uncertainties. By requiring agents to provide a single workflow that is evaluated across these "sealed worlds", we are able to test the accuracy and robustness of the workflows. We demonstrate the approach on four tasks built from CMS open data and present it as a way to reliably benchmark scientific work in experimental high-energy physics. At the time of writing, the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, reaches 60% of the score of the expert reference analyses on average, ahead of GPT 6 Astra at 38% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 31%. In individual sessions on one of the tasks, Gemini 4 Argon exceeds the reference. The benchmark is hosted at https://hep-ex-bench.github.io

items.title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
items.summary: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment.…
items.abstract: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

items.title: Interpretable Prototype-Conditioned Adaptation for Weather Forecasting
items.summary: Data-driven weather forecasting requires distinguishing local states and their temporal evolution. However, learned patterns remain implicit in neural forecasters, making their influence difficult to interpret.…
items.aiSummary: Group-specific prototype banks with cross-variable attention and sparse low-rank corrections improve the accuracy and interpretability of neural weather forecasting by explicitly linking local prototype contributions to prediction errors.
items.abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting requires distinguishing local states and their temporal evolution. However, learned patterns remain implicit in neural forecasters, making their influence difficult to interpret. Failing to distinguish local evolution can lead to similar forecasts for locations that develop differently, increasing prediction error. This motivates explicit references for distinguishing and interpreting local patterns. Prototypes provide explicit pattern references, but sample- or task-level conditioning leaves open how to adapt to distinct locations and variable groups. To deal with this problem, we design ProtoCast, which uses group-specific prototype banks to adapt local features while accounting for cross-variable dependencies. Specifically, (1) we combine each group's historical features and temporal change with forecast context from cross-variable attention for evolution-aware prototype matching. (2) Sparse mixtures of prototype-specific low-rank operators tailor corrections to each group and location. A gated attention block then exchanges the corrected features across groups before prediction. Each group's correction decomposes into explicit prototype contributions before this fusion. (3) We jointly train the forecasting network and operators from scratch and refit each group's prototypes before every training epoch. Slot tracking preserves prototype-operator associations, making each prototype's contribution to local corrections more interpretable. Experiments on GlobalForecast and TyphoonTracking show improved forecasting accuracy, while prototype deletion links local feature contributions to changes in prediction error. This work advances the development of more accurate and interpretable data-driven weather forecasting models. Project page: https://zhixuanli.github.io/projects/li2026protocast

items.title: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer: A Payment Foundation Model
items.summary: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model…
items.abstract: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model contains approximately 7B parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated per task route. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer is pretrained to learn reusable behavioral and relational representations, primarily on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on different merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on Ant International's billion-scale payment platform, the model reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online.

items.title: LoopedWAM: Looped World Action Models for Elastic Inference
items.summary: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present…
items.abstract: World action models (WAMs) couple generative video modeling with robotic action prediction but typically require large video and action transformers, limiting deployment efficiency. We present LoopedWAM, a compact WAM that recurrently applies a shared six-block core in each expert, executing 30 transformer layers while storing only 12 blocks per expert. To account for their asymmetric inference costs, the video and action experts can operate at different depths: visual features are computed once per query, whereas action computation repeats at every sampling step. We further propose elastic self-distillation, which trains a single elastic checkpoint, LoopedWAM-E, across action-depth and sampling-step budgets. With only 0.58B policy parameters and no robot pretraining, LoopedWAM achieves 96.1% success on LIBERO, 91.9% on RoboTwin 2.0, and 52.2% on RoboCasaGR1, while using 7.4times less peak GPU memory than Fast-WAM under matched inference measurements. On LIBERO, LoopedWAM-E achieves 96.0% success in 27.6 ms or 95.2% in 24.7 ms on an H100, providing multiple accuracy-latency operating points from a single checkpoint; with two sampling steps and four action loops, it stays within 0.5 points of LoopedWAM on all three benchmarks. Ablations demonstrate that weight-shared depth preserves competitive performance, while aggressive action-depth reduction requires explicit budget-aware training. On a real AgileX PiPER arm, LoopedWAM succeeds in 71.3% of 80 trials across four tasks.

items.title: Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences
items.summary: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations…
items.abstract: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.

items.title: Beam Model Technical Report
items.summary: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads.…
items.aiSummary: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts language model optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads, using large-scale asynchronous reinforcement learning, long-context midtraining, quantization, and speculative decoding to deliver strong reasoning and safety with efficient inference.
items.abstract: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features a 1M-token context window achieved through a novel two-stage midtraining phase, built on verifiable, correctness-anchored data. Post-training leveraged a large-scale, fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) campaign across 10.5K GB300 GPUs, generating over 100M rollouts over 4 weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of a plateau. Supported by deep hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2), Beam maximizes serving throughput with efficient, flexible deployment. Averaged across conversation turns and harm categories, Beam refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests, achieving the highest refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests among open-weight models on the Pareto frontier.

items.releaseNotes:
# v0.34.0 **1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new).** Thank you! ## TL;DR - **10 new models** (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!) - **Extensible KV cache is on by default:** vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now **remove `gpu_memory_utilization`** from your configs. - **Model Runner V1 is gone.** Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner. - **Big speedups** on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3). - **Upgrade check:** default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and `huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0` is required. See [Before you upgrade](#before-you-upgrade). ## Before you upgrade > [!IMPORTANT] > These changes can break existing setups. | Change | What to do | PR | |---|---|---| | Model Runner V1 removed | Remove `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0`; it now fails at startup. Port V1 logits processors to `vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor`. | #63373 | | Default `--block-size` is 64 (was 16) | Pass `--block-size 16` to keep the old behavior. ROCm paged attention still uses 16. | #63231 | | Extensible KV cache on by default; `gpu_memory_utilization` defaults to 1.0 | **In most cases it's now best to not set `gpu_memory_utilization`**. This should provide maximum kv cache capacity while avoiding runtime OOMs. Use it to share a GPU with other processes or when extensible kv cache is disabled. | #56492 | | ROCm 7.2 artifacts dropped | Use the ROCm 10.0 wheels and images. `-rocm72` is no longer published. | #61939 | | `huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0` required | Also requires `tokenizers >= 0.23.3` and `timm >= 1.0.30`. | #64779 | | QuTLASS / `fp_quant` removed | `fp_quant` checkpoints no longer load. | #65230 | | Marlin W4A8 removed | Use `--quantization humming` with `VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG` instead of `VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE`. | #65542 | | Keye-VL and Keye-VL-1.5 removed | — | #64287 | All breaking changes, deprecations and new defaults are listed in [the full changelog](#full-changelog). ## New models | Model | Notes | PR | |---|---|---| | **Mistral Large 4** | 1T total / 52B active, FP8 and NVFP4. Runs on NVIDIA Blackwell/Hopper and AMD MI350. | #64534 | | MiniMax-M3.1-Flash | Blackwell NVFP4 and ROCm kernels, DSpark draft | #64111 | | NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe | 30B-A4B speech model: audio chat and `/v1/audio/transcriptions` | #64282 | | Ricursive Ripple-65B Preview | BF16 and NVFP4, `ripple` reasoning and tool parsers | #65745 | | Zyphra ZAYA1 | ZAYA1-8B, ZAYA1-74B-preview | #65302 | | Baidu Unlimited-OCR-2 | DASH sparse attention | #64016 | | Liquid AI LFM3, LFM3-VL, LFM3-Audio | | #65826, #65827, #65828 | | NVIDIA Canary-1B-v2 | ASR and X↔En translation | #64215 | | Ming3-ASR | | #63585 | | NVIDIA Parakeet TDT | Through the vllm-parakeet-plugin | #65005 | ## Highlights ### Extensible KV cache, on by default - On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free **after** CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492). - **Result:** a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency. - **Trade-off:** per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.9` or `--no-enable-extensible-kv-cache`. - Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674). ### Model Runner V2 only - Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373). - Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464). ### Speculative decoding - **Suffix decoding** runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339). - **Custom speculators:** declarative configs plus a `register_speculative_method` plugin API (#63205). - **CUDA graphs** for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989). - **Adaptive verification** works with XPress (#65175). - **Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype**, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198). ### Performance | Improvement | Hardware | Gain | PR | |---|---|---|---| | Step5 NVFP4 MoE on TRTLLM-Gen | 4×GB200 | up to **1.95×** decode | #65152 | | GLM-5.3-Flash DeepGEMM FP8 MegaMoE | NVIDIA | **1.6×** output throughput vs DEP4 | #60895 | | Muse Spark Open specialized decode (opt-in) | GB300 | **1.5×** single-stream decode | #64077 | | Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill under TP (default) | GB200 | GLM-5.3 TTFT **1.24–1.40×** faster at 32K–128K | #63956 | | KV-balanced MLA decode for Kimi-K3 (opt-in) | GB300 | **1.34–1.59×** decode attention | #63638 | | Qwen3.5 on breakable CUDA graphs (no torch.compile) | NVIDIA | **3.0–8.8%** lower decode ITL | #51012 | | FlyDSL decode monokernel, Muse Spark Open DSpark | 8×MI355X | **+35–57%** interactivity at conc. 1–8 | #63440 | ### AMD ROCm - Release images and wheels are **ROCm 10.0 only** (#61939). - MoRI EPv2 via `--all2all-backend mori` (#61361). - Kimi-K3 specialized decode on MI355X, opt-in (#61435). - TRITON_ATTN is the default attention backend on RDNA3 and RDNA4 (#60418). ### Serving and operations - **Checkpoint/restore** (CRIU + `cuda-checkpoint`) through `/checkpoint/prepare`, `/checkpoint/status` and `/checkpoint/restore`, in both the Python and Rust frontends (#62570). - **Fault-tolerant DP+EP scale-down:** dead ranks are removed and their experts redistributed without a restart (#46370). - Best-effort **NUMA binding** on by default (#61258). - Opt-in **cache-aware admission** ordering (#54625). - Rust frontend: stateless **Responses API** (#63902) and **`n > 1`** (#65625). ## Install **Python wheels** | Platform | Install | |---|---| | CUDA 13.0 (PyPI) | `pip install vllm` | | CUDA 13.0 (uv) | `uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto` | | ROCm 10.0 | `pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/rocm/0.34.0/rocm100` | | XPU | `uv pip install vllm --extra-index-url https://wheels.vllm.ai/0.34.0/xpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu --index-strategy unsafe-best-match` | **Docker images** | Platform | Image | Short alias | |---|---|---| | CUDA 13.0 (default) | `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0` | | CUDA 13.0 + DeepEP over AWS EFA | `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.34.0-efa` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-efa` | | ROCm 10.0 | `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-rocm` | | CPU | `vllm/vllm-openai-cpu:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-cpu` | | XPU | `vllm/vllm-openai-xpu:v0.34.0` | `vllm/vllm:v0.34.0-xpu` | `latest` tags work the same way (e.g. `vllm/vllm:latest-rocm`). The default CUDA image now includes the AWS EFA userspace (libfabric, aws-ofi-nccl). The `-efa` image adds DeepEP built for EFA and routes NCCL over EFA by default (#65576). The **Assets** section below has the source tarball and the CUDA 13.0 (x86_64, arm64), CPU (x86_64, arm64, macOS) and XPU (x86_64) wheels. ## Full changelog
Model support - **Mistral Large 4** (#64534) runs on MRV2 with: - sparse MLA plus the DSA indexer, and cross-layer KV sharing; - DSpark, DCP/PCP, NIXL P/D and HiSparse. - **Other new models:** - MiniMax-M3.1-Flash (#64111), plus P/D across different prefill and decode TP (#64475). - Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe with MTP and DFlash2 (#64282, #64944). - **DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1** - Prefill gathers compressed KV once per KV-source group: 38 → 4 gathers per step (#59131). - Decoder replay graphs share the model graph pool: prefill graph memory 15.52 → 9.88 GiB per rank on GB200 (#63155). - `fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant` 3.5× faster, prefill 6% faster (#63540). - DSpark/MTP memory savings of about 512 MiB per GPU (#63996). - Engram host tables shared across DP ranks (#62359). - DeepGEMM sparse MQA logits on the FP8 indexer cache (#62011). - Packed multi-image vision encoding, 1.6–2.6× (#65030). - LoRA on the language model, compressor and `wo_a` layers (#57245, #64880). - DSpark with PCP (#61994); temporarily about 11% less KV cache and 25% lower image throughput). - Matryoshka dimensions for EmbeddingGemma 2 (#64885, #60978); RADIO C-RADIO v2/v3/v4 (#58468). - Qwen3-ASR on the upstream Transformers config; no `--hf-overrides` needed for the ForceAligner (#66097, #63274). - Fixes: GPT-OSS MXFP4 LoRA (#65825), PLaMo3 GPTQ (#62836), Ling3 (#65088), DomynEdge (#66819). - **Multimodal** - Encoder CUDA graphs for Pixtral/Mistral3 (#56277), shared capture buffers (#65084), one replay per batch up to `encoder_cudagraph_max_token_budget` (#65227). - On-device input normalization for Nemotron VL (#57924), Gemma 3 (#64487), Gemma 4 (#65577). - `--mm-encoder-tp-mode data` for MiMo-V2.6 (#64179). - Fixes: FlashInfer ViT attention on GLM-4.1V/GLM-OCR/GLM-5.3-Flash (#65778), Qwen3-Omni and Qwen2.5-Omni video budgets (#66017, #66190), dots_ocr with TP (#64543), embedding-only startup (#65689), media cache eviction (#65363).
Engine core - **Extensible KV cache** - On by default on CUDA and ROCm (#56492). - Headroom for measured allocator fragmentation, validated on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 at TP8+EP on 8×H200 (#67296). - Fixes: sizing and startup OOMs (#67485, #66523, #66731, #66197, #65554), connectors that failed to start (#65225), up to 84% undersized caches on DGX Spark (#65413), `--max-model-len auto` (#65463). - Startup warning when an explicit `gpu_memory_utilization` withholds memory from it (#66704); docs on when to set it (#67071). - **Model Runner V2** - The only runner after MRV1's removal (#63373); DBO with spec decode and DCP (#61464). - Separate prefill (token) and decode (request) CUDA graph capture sizes (#63406). - Staged writes copied straight into UVA (#63633); idle sampler writes skipped, about 10–11% faster small-batch decode (#62748). - Sampler warmed up after graph capture to stop memory growth under load (#62560). - Lower peak memory for chunked prompt logprobs (#64841, #64914); Triton ReplaySSM (#65033). - NVIDIA Confidential Computing decode fixes (#59981). - **Speculative decoding** - Suffix decoding (#60339) and custom speculators (#63205) on MRV2; draft-model CUDA graphs (#60989). - XPress with adaptive verification (#65175); adaptive verification draft budgets on a Triton kernel (#63421). - Batch-sharded draft logits (#63554); DSpark sequential blocks (#63886). - DSpark sliding-window MLA draft layers (#63795) under DCP (#63796); fused Markov sampling, 42–50% less sampling time (#64476); `draft_lm_head_quantization` (#64368). - Draft KV cache dtype aligned with the target (#65198). - Trace replay with ngram/EAGLE3/MTP, 1.47–2.03× (#63275); 3× faster resample kernel (#65100). - Fixes: DFlash acceptance of 0 with FULL CUDA graphs (#64059), a resample race (#66048), acceptance-estimator cancellation (#65229), standalone draft prefill under FULL graphs (#65804), grammar-invalid drafts (#61557). - **Scheduler and engine overhead** - Prompt token ids kept as int32 buffers: 40× less per-request CPU on a 128K prompt (#62702). - Per-request id lists kept out of the cyclic GC (#65300); 45–50% less KV block allocation CPU (#65831). - New requests and aborts handled while waiting for model output (#65466), with a cheaper wait loop (#65773). - Opt-in cache-aware admission via `--cache-aware-admission-window` (#54625). - `--max-num-inflight-kv-loads` starts async KV loads while the batch is full (#65319), with cached reservations: 47.2 → 5.4 ms per schedule (#65285). - A multimodal item is no longer split by a prefix hit (#65271). - **Startup and compile** - No openai/fastapi imports in EngineCore and workers (#65423, #65589). - CUDA graph memory profile skipped when its estimate is disabled (#64622). - Device-neutral compile cache via `VLLM_COMPILE_ON_ONE_RANK`, on by default (#63247); all graph-affecting config fields hashed into compile cache keys (#65652). - `--shuffle-safetensors-files` for large EP startups (#42837). - `BasevLLMParameter`'s Python `__torch_function__` dropped: GLM-5.2-FP8 TTFT −6.1% on GB300 (#63785). - **Lifecycle** - Process checkpoint/restore over HTTP (#62570); opt-in multi-worker CUDA checkpoint sleep (#64186). - Best-effort NUMA binding by default; `--no-numa-bind` to disable (#61258). - Sleep mode with exact-size pinned backups, up to about 578 GiB less host memory per node on Mistral Large 4 TP8 (#64630); level 2 discards only parameters (#66010, #6616

items.releaseNotes: # Release v5.23.0 ## New Model additions ### Inkling2 Inkling 2 Small is a multimodal model from Thinking Machines Lab that accepts text and image inputs and generates text outputs, and it is intended for use in English and other languages and across multiple coding languages. Its language backbone has 48 mixture-of-experts decoder layers, each routing tokens to 8 of 384 experts, for 594B total and 17B active parameters. It keeps the Inkling decoder (learned relative attention, short causal convolutions, mixture-of-experts layers) and adds block attention residuals, gated attention with a learned sink, and dynamic key/value convolutions. Images are encoded by a Perception Encoder-based vision transformer and projected into the language model embeddings, one embedding per 40x40 pixel patch. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/inkling2) | [Blog Post](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-small/) * Add inkling2 (#50682) by @guarin in [#50682](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/50682) ### JEV JEV is a decision head that scores single-token labels with a linear layer at the last token of the prompt, soft-capped like the logits of a language model head. `JevForDecision` is the model of the checkpoint and its head, and it reads the head files shipped next to the weights (`head.safetensors` and `judge_config.json` for JEV). The same head is also used by GEV and reads the 255 answer codes of pplx-decider and d3, and it can be run through the experimental `decision` pipeline or directly with `decide`. **Note:** JEV and the decision pipeline are currently experimental. Their APIs, configuration, and behavior may change as development continues. They should be used with caution in production environments. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/jev) * Add Jev + decision core (#50054) by @ArthurZucker in [#50054](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/50054) ### LFM3 LFM3 is the third generation of Liquid Foundation Models from Liquid AI. Like LFM2, it is a hybrid architecture that combines gated short convolutions with grouped-query attention, with the attention layers split between full-attention and sliding-window layers. The attention layers apply RMSNorm to the query and key heads and gate their output with a per-head sigmoid. Every layer applies a sandwich norm to the operator and feed-forward outputs before the residual addition. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/lfm3) * [Model] LFM3 Family: LFM3-Text (#50322) by @paulpak58 in [#50322](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/50322) ### Dots 3 Note Preview Dots 3 Note Preview is a mixture-of-experts causal language model that accepts native text, image, video, and audio inputs. It uses a shared vision encoder for images and videos and a Whisper-style audio encoder, and both encoders project their outputs into the language model's hidden space before autoregressive text generation. BF16 and FP8 inference are supported. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/dots3_note) * Add dots3-note Preview model support (#47844) by @miraclezqc in [#47844](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/47844) ### LFM3-VL LFM3-VL is a vision-language model family from Liquid AI, built on the LFM3 language model. It takes images and videos at their native resolution together with text. It combines a hybrid vision encoder (a linear patchifier, gated depthwise 2D convolution layers, and bidirectional grouped-query attention layers with 2D rotary embeddings) with a projector and an LFM3 language model. The projector merges each 2x2 block of patch features into one language token through a layer norm and a two-layer MLP. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/lfm3_vl) * [Model] LFM3 Family: LFM3-VL (#50392) by @paulpak58 in [#50392](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/50392) ### IQuestCoder IQuest-Coder-V1 is a family of code language models developed by IQuest Lab, available in 7B, 14B and 40B sizes with base, instruct and thinking variants. Its architecture is the same as Llama, so the Transformers auto classes load it with LlamaModel and LlamaForCausalLM, and only IQuestCoderConfig is specific to IQuestCoder. The looped `IQuest-Coder-V1-*-Loop-*` checkpoints use a different architecture and aren't supported. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/iquestcoder) * Add IQuestCoder (#50579) by @hmellor in [#50579](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/50579) ### InternLM3 InternLM3 is an 8B instruction-tuned language model developed by Shanghai AI Laboratory (checkpoint: internlm/internlm3-8b-instruct). Its architecture is the same as Llama, so the auto classes load it with the Llama implementation (LlamaModel and LlamaForCausalLM), and only InternLM3Config is specific to InternLM3. The config names the attention biases `qkv_bias` and the output projection and MLP biases `bias`. InternLM3Config loads these as `attention_bias` and `mlp_bias` and requires them to be equal, as they are in the released checkpoints. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/internlm3) * Add InternLM3 (#50578) by @hmellor in [#50578](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/50578) ## Breaking changes * 🚨 Remove the `ep_router` expert-parallel style (#49615) by @IlyasMoutawwakil * 🚨 Run MXFP4 GPT-OSS experts through `ep_dispatch_experts` (#49613) by @IlyasMoutawwakil * 🚨 `deepgemm_megamoe` EP implementation for DeepGEMM Mega MoE (#49606) by @IlyasMoutawwakil * 🚨 Slim down `[audio]` to torchaudio + soundfile + soxr (drop librosa and phonemizer) (#50610) by @eustlb * 🚨 Deprecate Wav2Vec2ProcessorWithLM and pyctcdecode/kenlm LM decoding (#50408) by @eustlb * 🚨 Exporters: `ExportedModel`, Hub save/load, one backend registry (#50029) by @IlyasMoutawwakil * 🚨 Move processing defaults to class (#49089) by @guarin * :rotating_light: [`kernels`] Bump version (#50307) by @vasqu * :rotating_light: Finally drop rope deltas from ModelOutput! (#50153) by @zucchini-nlp * 🚨 Safe-ize pi0 graphs (#50160) by @molbap * 🚨 [serve][breaking] update attn for mac users (#49730) by @SunMarc * 🚨 build and expand once the tp/ep_plan/fsdp_plan (#49527) by @3outeille ## Exporters: export, share and run any model on its backend (#50029, #50032, #50309, #50311) https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2b17b2ab-b2b8-4e34-a983-4a7177330e4e Every export now returns an `ExportedModel`. You call it like the original model (same kwargs, same output class), push it to the Hub, and load it back on the backend's own runtime. The same API covers Dynamo, ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO and ExecuTorch. ```python from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer from transformers.exporters import ExportedModel, OnnxConfig, OnnxExporter model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("google/embeddinggemma-2") tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("google/embeddinggemma-2") inputs = tokenizer(["Exporters are here!"], return_tensors="pt") exported = OnnxExporter().export(model, inputs, OnnxConfig(dynamic=True, ort_fusions="cuda")) exported.push_to_hub("my-org/embeddinggemma-2-onnx") exported_model = ExportedModel.from_pretrained("my-org/embeddinggemma-2-onnx", device="cuda") outputs = exported_model(**inputs) # same output class as model(**inputs) ``` - **Fused for the runtime**: `OnnxConfig(ort_fusions="cpu" | "cuda" | "webgpu" | "dml")` rewrites the graph into ONNX Runtime's fused transformer ops at export time: attention, `GroupQueryAttention` over the KV cache, rotary, norms and `MoE`. OpenVINO exports now hit OpenVINO's fused CPU kernels for attention, RoPE, MoE experts and compressed int8/int4 weights, which makes decode 2.4–3.9× faster than before. - **Faster than `torch.compile`**: on EmbeddingGemma2 (8 × 128 tokens), ONNX Runtime with the TensorRT EP is 7.6× faster than eager PyTorch and 1.4× faster than `torch.compile` on an A100. OpenVINO is 4.1× faster than eager and 2.2× faster than `torch.compile` on a Xeon Platinum 8570 (4.9× and 2.6× with int8 weights). - **Shareable**: an export saves and loads like a model, optionally in a `subfolder` of the model repo. Its `export.json` records the config, input shapes, package versions and I/O names. Quantized exports (PT2E, NNCF, ONNX Runtime) save and run the same way. 🚨 `export()` returns an `ExportedModel`, and an ONNX program is an `onnx_ir.Model`. `OnnxConfig`'s and `OpenVINOConfig`'s `output_path` options are gone in favour of `save_pretrained`. Custom backends register with `register_backend`. 📚 Docs: https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/exporters ## Vision This release fixes a range of vision-model bugs: classification pipelines now respect `problem_type`, and several models get corrected behavior (Step3.7 RoPE axis order, MiniMax-M3-VL packed attention isolation, Qwen VL positions with reused caches, PaddleOCR-VL interpolation alignment, Kosmos2 SDPA masking, and Emu3 float image handling). Chunked prefill now keeps image inputs on the * fix(pipelines): respect problem_type in image and video classification pipelines (#50582) by @surendra902 in [#50582] * Fix Step3.7 vision RoPE spatial W/H axis order (#50547) by @caohch-1 in [#50547] * Raise ValueError for out-of-range float images in convert_to_rgb (#50487) by @n24q02m in [#50487] * CI: install OpenVINO and NNCF in the daily GPU image (#50422) by @IlyasMoutawwakil in [#50422] * Fix MiniMax-M3-VL packed vision attention isolation (#50346) by @taking-lying-flat in [#50346] * Fix Qwen VL positions when a text cache is reused with a new image (#50427) by @Arnav66692 in [#50427] * [Docker] Update Nvidia CI and Flash Attn CI images to torch 2.15 / cu132 (#50467) by @ydshieh in [#50467] * Fix PaddleOCR-VL vision position interpolation alignment (#50384) by @scyyh11 in [#50384] * Fix Emu3 image processor crash on float numpy images (#50226) by @simpleqt in [#50226] * Build Idefics-style vision position ids with torch.where (#49917) by @shoumikhin in [#49917] * Keep image inputs on the first chunk of a chunked prefill (#49753) by @digit50 in [#49753] * Docs: note in the v5 migration guide that hidden_states[-1] of vision models is pre-norm (#50303) by @ravediamond in [#50303] * Remove the GitHub API cache-bust from the AMD docker images (#49351) by @tarekziade in [#49351] * [docs] Vision backend differences (#50131) by @stevhliu in [#50131] * [Kosmos2] Fix SDPA applying a causal mask in the image-to-text projection (#50118) by @tarekziade in [#50118] ## Parallelization This release improves distributed training and inference. Expert parallelism gains a selectable `ep_implementation` (all-reduce for CUDA-graph-friendly inference, all-to-all for training). The Trainer now reduces FSDP/HSDP gradients only on the last micro-batch, and the token-count normalization is fixed to use true division. Tensor-parallel fixes cover attention sinks (including Beam attention) and tied-weight comparisons on TPU * Expert-parallel implementations for `ep_dispatch_experts`: all-reduce at inference, all-to-all in training (#49429) by @IlyasMoutawwakil in [#49429] * [FSDP tests] Fork CPU ranks from a forkserver instead of spawning them (#50444) by @ydshieh in [#50444] * [distributed - TPU] Fix tied-weight comparisons on TPUs when using TP (#50406) by @tengomucho in [#50406] * [`distributed`] Trainer: reduce FSDP/HSDP gradients on the last micro-batch only (#50286) by @3outeille in [#50286] * Update FSDP non-rank-0 missing keys test after #45649 (#50260) by @SunMarc in [#50260] * [`Beam`] Fix TP on attn (#50302) by @vasqu in [#50302] * Fix/trainer parallel token count 50212 (#50214) by @BlazeSR10hawk in [#50214] * Reuse the TP/EP test ranks across tests instead of spawning them per test (#49986) by @3outeille in [#49986] * handle local sink in TP (#49567) by @3outeille in [#49567] ## Cache This release fixes several cache correctness issues: static-cache prefill attention in Gemma4's KV-shared layers, Qwen VL positions when a cache is reused with a new image or video, and DeepSeek-V4 compression-state reordering during beam search. It also improves cache sharing for Mistral Large 4 and adds OpenVINO export fusion for the KV cache and attention. Smaller changes cover CI and test fixes, including vLLM CI memory * Gemma4: fix static cache attending to empty cache slots in KV-shared layers at prefill (#50528) by @ydshieh in [#50528] * vLLM CI: fix install and KV-cache memory, add failure report job (#50436) by @ydshieh in [#50436] * Fix DeepSeek-V4 compression cache reordering for beam search (#50348) by @taking-lying-flat in [#50348] * OpenVINO exporter: let OpenVINO fuse attention, RoPE, the KV cache and compressed matmuls (#50311) by @IlyasMoutawwakil in [#50311] * [tests] Pin the chat-template date in Llama's FA static-cache test (#50296) by @tarekziade in [#50296] * Fix a cache test (#50320) by @Cyrilvallez in [#50320] * Improve Mistral Large 4 cache sharing (#50305) by @Cyrilvallez in [#50305] ## Kernels This release fixes several hub kernel issues: the MPS RMSNorm kernel repo id was corrected, the MegaBlocksMoeMLP mapping was restored for MXFP4 GPT-OSS, and a failed flash-attention kernel load is now retried instead of leaving models unregistered. It also raises the minimum `kernels` version (fixing ROCm issues and a multi-GPU bug), bumps mamba-ssm kernels to v4 * Fix the MPS RMSNorm hub kernel repo id (#50714) by @tarekziade in [#50714] * [`GptOss`] Fix the kernels autodispatch test (#50630) by @vasqu in [#50630] * [`kernels`] Bump min version (#50509) by @vasqu in [#50509] * Retry the attention kernel load after a failed `lazy_import_flash_attention` (#50391) by @albertvillanova in [#50391] * Test the dispatched FA3 kernel per device (#50304) by @Abdennacer-Badaoui in [#50304] * upgrade version for mamba-ssm and fla kernel (#50294) by @kaixuanliu in [#50294] * Restore the `MegaBlocksMoeMLP` hub kernel mapping for MXFP4 GPT-OSS (#50150) by @jiqing-feng in [#50150] ## Attention This release fixes a range of attention bugs: vision-attention isolation in MiniMax-M3-VL, SDPA decode under `torch.compile`, eager NaNs in Qwen4-Exp with left padding, an unintended causal mask in Kosmos-2's SDPA projection, and default full-attention mask selection that wrongly picked linear layers. It also retries failed attention kernel loads, excludes padding from the repetition penalty, and lets the O * [`SDPA`] Fix decode under compile (#50388) by @vasqu in [#50388] * Exclude attention-masked padding from repetition penalty (#50149) by @BlazeSR10hawk in [#50149] * Fix Qwen4-Exp eager attention NaNs with left padding (#49923) by @taking-lying-flat in [#49923] * [Masking] Skip linear layers for the default full-attention mask (#50059) by @paulpak58 in [#50059] ## Generation This release fixes several generation bugs: padded generation in RecurrentGemma, batched decoding in Falcon-H1, beam search cache reordering in DeepSeek-V4, and batched metadata and beam scores in `TextGenerationPipeline`. It also lets an unchanged `GenerationConfig` be saved without strict-validation errors, avoids copying the KV cache when decoding with grouped-query attention (GQA), and fixes an `Attribut * Fix RecurrentGemma padded generation by declaring its `layer_types` (#50577) by @ydshieh
